feedback.problem: What is the coefficient of ${(x-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}$ in the second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)$ at $x=\frac{1}{3}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=\frac{1}{3}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =f(\frac{1}{3})+{f}^{′}(\frac{1}{3})(x-\frac{1}{3})+\frac{{f}^{″}(\frac{1}{3})}{2}{(x-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of ${(x-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}$ in the above Taylor polynomial is 

$$
\frac{{f}^{″}(\frac{1}{3})}{2}.
$$

To find this coefficient, we start by computing the second derivative ${f}^{″}(x):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x) \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x) \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-4{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=\frac{1}{3}.$ This gives

$$
{f}^{″}(\frac{1}{3})=-4{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})=-4{\pi }^{2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})=2{\pi }^{2}.
$$

Finally, we determine the coefficient of ${(x-\frac{1}{3})}^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{″}(\frac{1}{3})}{2} & =\frac{2{\pi }^{2}}{2}={\pi }^{2}\end{aligned}
$$
